CN.q: In a star topology, what is the single point of failure?
opts: There is no single point of failure
CN.exp: If the central device fails, the entire star network fails; a single cable failure only disconnects one node.

CN.q: Which topology forms a single continuous path with no central server, used in SONET/SDH networks?
CN.exp: Ring topology connects each node to exactly two neighbours forming a continuous loop; SONET and SDH are classic examples.

CN.q: A fully connected mesh of n nodes requires how many point-to-point links?
CN.exp: Each node connects to every other node: nC2 = n(n-1)/2 links, which is why mesh cabling cost is high.

CN.q: Tree topology is best described as a combination of which two topologies?
CN.exp: Tree (expanded star) topology connects multiple star networks to a single backbone bus, typically using Ethernet.

CN.q: In bus topology, when a device transmits data, the data is:
opts: Sent only to the recipient's port
Sent to all devices attached to the bus
Sent to the central hub only
CN.exp: The bus is a shared communication medium; the transmitted signal reaches every attached device, which then discards it if not addressed to itself.

CN.q: What is the main drawback of a bus topology?
opts: If the bus is damaged, the whole network fails
CN.exp: The central cable is a single point of failure; any damage to the bus brings down the entire network.

CN.q: Mesh topology has two variants. Which is correct?
CN.exp: Fully connected mesh: every node connected to every other. Partially connected mesh: not all pairs are directly linked.

CN.q: Which topology results when a star topology is connected to a different topology?
CN.exp: Combining different topologies produces a hybrid topology; joining two star topologies just yields another star.

CN.q: If the 'main bus' in a tree topology breaks:
opts: Only the root star is affected
CN.exp: Tree topology depends on the main bus/backbone; damage to it brings the whole network down.

CN.q: Which network type would connect branch offices of a company across cities of a country?
CN.exp: A WAN spans wide geographical areas such as cities and countries; a MAN is limited to a single metropolitan city.

CN.q: What is the approximate range limit of a PAN (Personal Area Network)?
CN.exp: A PAN's range limit is roughly 10 metres — Bluetooth-style personal device networks.

CN.q: A CAN (Campus Area Network) is best described as:
opts: A network within a single building
A connection of devices within a campus linking multiple departments
CN.exp: A CAN links devices across a campus area (e.g., a university) covering multiple departments/buildings.

CN.q: Which network uses satellites to connect devices over the global area?
CN.exp: A GAN (Global Area Network) uses satellite links to provide worldwide connectivity.

CN.q: A HAN (House Area Network) is essentially:
opts: A LAN used within a house to connect home devices
CN.exp: A HAN is a LAN restricted to household use, connecting PCs, printers, phones and other home devices.

CN.q: A VPN is best described as:
opts: A private LAN with encrypted switches
A private WAN built over the public internet using a secure tunnel
A dedicated leased line between offices
CN.exp: A VPN creates a secure, encrypted tunnel across the public internet, giving remote users/offices private-network access cheaply compared to dedicated WAN links.

CN.q: Which VPN type is intended for remote/mobile individual employees rather than connecting whole office networks?
CN.exp: Access (remote-access) VPN serves telecommuters and mobile users; Site-to-Site (Intranet/Extranet) links entire office networks.

CN.q: An Intranet VPN is used to:
opts: Connect an organisation to its customers securely
Connect remote offices in different geographical locations using shared infrastructure with the same policies as a private WAN
CN.exp: Intranet VPN links remote offices of the same organisation via shared infrastructure, giving them WAN-like unified accessibility policies.

CN.q: An Extranet VPN differs from an Intranet VPN because it:
opts: Connects the organisation with external partners, suppliers, or customers via dedicated connections
Is limited to a single building
CN.exp: Extranet VPNs extend the intranet infrastructure to external stakeholders using dedicated, controlled connections.

CN.q: An IPv4 address is how many bits long, arranged as how many octets?
CN.exp: IPv4 addresses are 32-bit values written as four 8-bit octets (each 0–255).

CN.q: The IPv4 address 200.45.10.9 belongs to which class?
CN.exp: Class C spans 192.0.0.0 – 223.255.255.255; used for local area networks.

CN.q: Which IPv4 class is reserved for multicasting?
CN.exp: Class D (224.0.0.0 – 239.255.255.255) is reserved for multicast; Class E is kept for study/R&D.

CN.q: Which range covers Class A IPv4 addresses?
CN.exp: Class A: 0.0.0.0 to 127.255.255.255, used for very large networks.

CN.q: Which statement about public vs private IP addresses is correct?
opts: Private IPs are routable on the internet directly
Public IPs are assigned by the ISP and used on the internet; private IPs are not valid on the internet without NAT/proxy
Public and private IPs are interchangeable
CN.exp: Public IPs come from the ISP and are internet-routable; private IPs need NAT or a proxy to reach the internet.

CN.q: Which OSI layer converts data into frames, attaches MAC addresses, and performs flow/error control on a link?
CN.exp: Framing, physical addressing, flow control, error control and link management are data-link-layer functions.

CN.q: Routing, logical addressing, packetizing and fragmentation are functions of which OSI layer?
CN.exp: The network layer determines the best source-to-destination route, assigns logical (IP) addresses, packetizes data and fragments packets.

CN.q: Which OSI layer is called the 'Translation layer' and handles data compression and encryption?
CN.exp: The presentation layer translates between application format and common network format, and handles character code translation, compression and encryption.

CN.q: Which OSI layer transmits the raw bitstream over a physical medium?
CN.exp: The physical layer is the lowest layer, handling unstructured raw-bit transmission over cables/wireless media.

CN.q: Beginning, maintaining and ending communication sessions between devices is the job of which layer?
CN.exp: The session layer establishes, maintains and terminates sessions between users, and reports errors from upper layers.

CN.q: A connection-oriented transmission where the receiver sends an acknowledgement is provided by which OSI layer?
CN.exp: The transport layer offers both connection-oriented (ack-based) and connectionless services and handles end-to-end error checking.

CN.q: The application layer of OSI enables the user to access the network. Which is a valid application-layer protocol?
CN.exp: HTTP, SMTP, DNS, FTP are all application-layer protocols; ARP is network-layer-adjacent, Ethernet is data-link, IP is network.

CN.q: The TCP/IP reference model has how many layers, and which layer 'holds the architecture together' by delivering IP packets?
CN.exp: TCP/IP has 4 layers (Link, Internet, Transport, Application); the Internet layer (IP, ICMP) delivers packets end-to-end.

CN.q: In the TCP/IP model, which layer decides which physical links (e.g., serial lines, Ethernet) meet the needs of the connectionless internet layer?
CN.exp: The Link layer chooses link technology (Ethernet, Sonet, etc.) to satisfy the connectionless Internet layer above it.

CN.q: Which statement about HTTP vs HTTPS is correct?
opts: HTTP uses port 443; HTTPS uses port 80
HTTPS adds SSL/TLS on top of HTTP and uses port 443 by default
HTTP is stateful; HTTPS is stateless
HTTPS works over UDP for speed
CN.exp: HTTPS is HTTP secured with SSL/TLS encryption, default port 443; plain HTTP is a stateless application-layer protocol on port 80.

CN.q: HTTP is called a 'stateless protocol' because:
opts: Each command is independent of previous commands
CN.exp: Stateless means the server treats every HTTP command as unrelated to earlier ones; state must be added externally (e.g., cookies).

CN.q: What does DNS primarily do?
opts: Assigns IP addresses dynamically to hosts
Maps domain names to their IP addresses
Encrypts traffic between browser and server
CN.exp: DNS resolves human-readable domain names into IP addresses. Dynamic IP assignment is DHCP's job.

CN.q: A DNS forwarder is used when:
opts: A client wants to bypass DNS caching
A DNS server forwards queries it cannot resolve to external DNS servers
A router converts MAC to IP addresses
CN.exp: A forwarder-configured DNS server passes unresolvable queries to external DNS servers for resolution.

CN.q: Which underlying transport does DNS typically use for its lookups?
CN.exp: DNS uses UDP for the vast majority of queries (fast, connectionless) and falls back to TCP for large responses/zone transfers.

CN.q: SMTP listens on which port, and what is it used for?
CN.exp: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) governs email transmission and is always listening on port 25.

CN.q: SMTP supports which two delivery methods?
CN.exp: SMTP supports both End-to-End (direct) and Store-and-Forward (via intermediate servers) email delivery.

CN.q: POP3 is responsible for:
opts: Accessing the mail service on a client machine
CN.exp: POP3 (Post Office Protocol v3) handles retrieving mail to a client machine, operating in Delete or Keep modes.

CN.q: Which is a key difference between TCP and UDP?
opts: UDP is connection-oriented; TCP is connectionless
TCP retransmits lost packets; UDP does not
UDP provides flow control and acknowledgements
CN.exp: TCP is connection-oriented with error checking, ACKs, flow control and retransmission; UDP is faster, simpler, and connectionless.

CN.q: Which protocol does 'basic checksum-only' error checking?
CN.exp: UDP has only checksum-based error detection; TCP performs extensive error checking with retransmissions and flow control.

CN.q: Which protocol auto-assigns IP addresses and other network configuration to devices?
CN.exp: DHCP (application layer) auto-configures IP, subnet mask and DNS details for hosts (default port 67).

CN.q: ARP is used to:
opts: Map an IP address to a MAC address
Map a MAC address to an IP address
Find the best route using hop count
CN.exp: Address Resolution Protocol converts a logical (IP) address into the device's physical (MAC) address on the local network.

CN.q: Which protocol is primarily used for error handling and diagnostics (e.g., 'ping')?
CN.exp: ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is a network-layer protocol used by routers for error reporting and connectivity diagnostics.

CN.q: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) selects the best route based on:
CN.exp: RIP is a dynamic routing protocol that uses hop-count as its metric; suited to small/medium networks.

CN.q: FTP is used to:
CN.exp: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is an application-layer protocol for reliable, efficient file transfer, including downloads from remote servers.

CN.q: Which statement about MAC and IP addresses is correct?
opts: Both are assigned by the ISP
MAC identifies the physical device (from the NIC manufacturer); IP identifies the network connection (from the ISP)
MAC changes with every network; IP is permanent
CN.exp: NIC manufacturers assign MAC addresses (hardware identity); ISPs assign IP addresses (network identity).

CN.q: Hub vs switch — which is correct?
opts: Hub is data-link and filters packets
Switch is physical and broadcasts to all ports
Hub is physical with no packet filtering; switch is data-link with packet filtering
Both operate at the network layer
CN.exp: A hub blindly repeats signals to every port (physical layer, no filtering); a switch is a full-duplex data-link-layer device that filters and forwards frames per port.

CN.q: A node that connects two or more networks and forwards messages between them is called:
CN.exp: Gateways/routers connect different networks, regulating and forwarding traffic between them.

CN.q: A NIC (Network Interface Card):
opts: Is a peripheral card that attaches a PC to a network and has its own MAC address
CN.exp: A NIC connects a PC to a network and carries a unique MAC address identifying that PC on the network.

CN.q: When you type google.com, what happens immediately after the OS resolves the IP via DNS?
opts: The browser renders the cached page
An HTTP request is sent without any connection
A TCP connection is established with the server using a three-way handshake
The server pushes the page via UDP
CN.exp: After DNS resolution: TCP three-way handshake → HTTP request → HTTP response → render (and cache if cacheable).

CN.q: Which delivery method targets a subset of nodes with the same data (used to send data to multiple selected receivers)?
CN.exp: Multicast targets a subset of receivers. Unicast: one node; anycast: any one of several servers; broadcast: all nodes.

CN.q: Which delivery method sends data to any one of several servers (used by CDNs)?
CN.exp: Anycast routes traffic to the topologically nearest instance among several, commonly used by CDNs and DNS root servers.

CN.q: A firewall's role is to:
opts: Monitor incoming/outgoing traffic and block based on security policies
CN.exp: A firewall (hardware, software, or both) sits between a private network and the public internet, enforcing security policies.

CN.q: VPN encrypts internet traffic to:
opts: Disguise online identity and protect confidentiality
CN.exp: A VPN protects confidentiality and hides the user's real IP/identity; it does not inherently increase throughput.

CN.q: Which are the elements of a protocol?
CN.exp: A protocol is defined by syntax (format), semantics (meaning), and timing (when/how fast data is sent).

CN.q: Network reliability is measured by all of these EXCEPT:
CN.exp: Reliability metrics per the notes: downtime (recovery time), failure frequency, and catastrophe robustness.

CN.q: Subnetting a network is done primarily to:
opts: Achieve higher routing efficiency and enhance security
CN.exp: Subnetting divides a network into subnets, improving routing efficiency and security, and reducing routing-table lookup time.

CN.q: Netstat is a utility that:
opts: Shows current TCP/IP connections and settings
CN.exp: Netstat is a command-line utility providing useful information about the current TCP/IP setting and active connections.

CN.q: Which command is used on Linux/UNIX/macOS to view and configure network interfaces?
CN.exp: ifconfig (Interface Configuration) is used on Linux/UNIX/macOS; ipconfig is the Windows equivalent.

CN.q: RAID stands for:
CN.exp: RAID = Redundant Array of Independent Disks — stores data redundantly across multiple drives for performance/fault tolerance (7 levels).

OS.q: An operating system is best defined as:
opts: An interface between the user/applications and hardware, managing resources
OS.exp: The OS is the interface between users/applications and hardware, responsible for process execution, resource allocation, CPU, file and memory management.

OS.q: In which OS type does the CPU switch to another job whenever the running process waits for I/O?
OS.exp: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in main memory; when the running process blocks for I/O, the OS assigns the CPU to another job.

OS.q: A time-sharing OS is characterised by:
opts: Interaction with the user (e.g., keyboard) with the OS responding to instructions
OS.exp: Time-sharing systems interact with users through input devices; the OS executes instructions and responds with output.

OS.q: A Real-Time OS is typically used when:
opts: Multiple users share a computer casually
Rigid, fixed timing constraints govern operations
OS.exp: Real-time systems have well-defined, fixed time constraints — used in dedicated systems that must meet deadlines.

OS.q: In a batch OS, a job is assigned to the CPU:
opts: When the previous job's execution completes
OS.exp: Batch OS stores similar jobs in memory; a new job takes the CPU only after the previous one finishes execution.

OS.q: Each process in an OS is represented by:
OS.exp: A PCB stores metadata about a process — including the program counter — used by the OS to manage the process.

OS.q: The program counter (PC) of a process indicates:
opts: Address of the next instruction to be executed
OS.exp: The PC value indicates the address of the next instruction of the process being executed.

OS.q: A process makes 4 fork() system calls. How many child processes are created?
OS.exp: n fork() calls generate 2^n − 1 children: 2^4 − 1 = 15.

OS.q: If Completion Time = 27 and Arrival Time = 5, Burst Time = 12, what is the Waiting Time?
OS.exp: Turnaround = 27 − 5 = 22; Waiting = Turnaround − Burst = 22 − 12 = 10.

OS.q: Turnaround Time is defined as:
OS.exp: Turnaround Time = Completion Time − Arrival Time.

OS.q: Waiting Time is defined as:
OS.exp: Waiting Time = Turnaround Time − Burst Time.

OS.q: Which resources does a thread NOT share with other threads of the same process?
opts: Its own stack and register set
OS.exp: Each thread has its own PC, register set, and stack; it shares the process's code, data, files and signals.

OS.q: Which pair is a valid classification of threads?
OS.exp: Threads are broadly user threads (implemented by user libraries) and kernel threads (implemented by the OS).

OS.q: Which of these is NOT typically an advantage of multithreaded programming?
OS.exp: Multithreading is responsive, economical, shares process resources and exploits multiprocessors, but does not itself prevent deadlocks.

OS.q: Which scheduling algorithm is the simplest and schedules based purely on arrival times?
OS.exp: First Come First Serve is the simplest algorithm; jobs are scheduled strictly in arrival order.

OS.q: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) is:
OS.exp: SRTF preempts the running process if a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining burst — the preemptive form of SJF.

OS.q: Round Robin scheduling gives each process:
opts: A fixed time slice in a cyclic order
OS.exp: RR assigns each process a fixed time quantum in a cyclic fashion, giving fair sharing among all processes.

OS.q: In non-preemptive priority scheduling, if two processes have equal priority, the tiebreaker is:
OS.exp: For equal priorities, scheduling defaults to arrival order.

OS.q: Which scheduling algorithm avoids starvation via a response ratio?
OS.exp: HRRN = (Waiting + Burst) / Burst — long waits raise the ratio, so long-waiting processes eventually get scheduled.

OS.q: In Multilevel Feedback Queue scheduling, a process that consumes too much CPU time is:
opts: Given a longer quantum in the same queue
OS.exp: MLFQ demotes CPU-hungry processes to lower-priority queues based on CPU-burst behaviour, unlike static MLQ.

OS.q: Which is NOT one of the three required conditions for a valid critical-section solution?
OS.exp: Solutions require mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. Circular wait is a deadlock condition.

OS.q: A race condition is:
opts: A process running faster than expected
When the final output depends on the order in which shared variables are accessed
Blocking on I/O for too long
OS.exp: Race conditions arise when the outcome depends on interleavings of accesses to shared variables.

OS.q: Bounded waiting guarantees:
opts: A process waits at most a fixed amount of wall-clock time
A bound exists on how many times other processes can enter the CS after one has requested it
OS.exp: Bounded waiting ensures a limit on how many times other processes may enter the critical section between a process's request and its grant.

OS.q: A semaphore whose value ranges over an unrestricted integer domain is a:
OS.exp: Counting semaphores take unrestricted integers; binary semaphores take only 0/1 and implement mutual exclusion.

OS.q: Binary semaphores are used to implement:
OS.exp: Binary semaphores (values 0/1) implement mutual exclusion and synchronise concurrent processes.

OS.q: A mutex differs from a counting semaphore in that:
opts: A mutex provides mutual exclusion — only one thread can hold it at a time
Mutex is only used in kernels
OS.exp: A mutex is a mutual-exclusion primitive; only one owner holds it at a time, generalisable via semaphores.

OS.q: Which set lists all four necessary conditions for deadlock?
opts: Mutual exclusion, hold & wait, preemption, circular wait
Mutual exclusion, hold & wait, no preemption, circular wait
Starvation, hold & wait, no preemption, aging
Mutual exclusion, race condition, no preemption, circular wait
OS.exp: Deadlock requires all four simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, NO preemption, circular wait.

OS.q: Windows and UNIX generally handle deadlock by:
OS.exp: Since deadlock is rare, both Windows and UNIX ignore it and rely on a reboot — the 'ignore altogether' strategy.

OS.q: Banker's algorithm is a technique for:
OS.exp: Banker's algorithm avoids deadlock — never allocating resources such that a safe sequence cannot be found.

OS.q: The 'Hold and Wait' condition means:
opts: Processes only wait, never hold resources
A process holds at least one resource while waiting for more
OS.exp: Hold and wait: a process is holding at least one resource while requesting additional resources.

OS.q: Overlays are best described as:
opts: Only keeping in memory the instructions/data needed at a given time
OS.exp: Overlays load only the instructions/data currently needed, letting a program larger than memory execute.

OS.q: Swapping in multiprogramming refers to:
opts: Moving a process out of memory when its time slice ends
OS.exp: Swapping moves processes that have used their time slice out of memory to disk to make room for others.

OS.q: In variable-partition allocation, which strategy leaves the LARGEST leftover hole after allocation?
OS.exp: Worst fit deliberately places the process in the hole that leaves the maximum gap.

OS.q: First fit allocates:
opts: The first hole in which the process fits completely
OS.exp: First fit scans free holes in order and allocates the first hole into which the process fits completely.

OS.q: Best fit chooses the hole that:
opts: Fits the process with the minimum leftover space
OS.exp: Best fit selects the hole in which the process fits with the least memory left over.

OS.q: External fragmentation in contiguous allocation is primarily solved by:
OS.exp: Paging removes the requirement of contiguous allocation by dividing memory into equal-size frames/pages.

OS.q: Internal fragmentation occurs in systems that use:
OS.exp: Fixed-size units (fixed partitions, pages) waste space inside an allocated block. Variable-size units cause external fragmentation.

OS.q: Segmentation differs from paging in that:
opts: Segmentation provides a user view; the logical address space is a collection of segments (of varying sizes)
OS.exp: Segmentation is user-oriented: logical space is a collection of variable-length segments; it may or may not use paging underneath.

OS.q: A page fault is:
opts: An error when a program accesses an invalid address
An interrupt raised when a referenced page is in the virtual space but not in physical memory
OS.exp: A page fault is a hardware interrupt when a referenced page is mapped in virtual memory but not present in physical memory.

OS.q: Belady's anomaly refers to:
opts: More page faults with more frames under LRU
More page faults with more frames under FIFO
Fewer page faults with fewer frames under Optimal
OS.exp: Under FIFO replacement, more frames can paradoxically increase page faults (Belady's anomaly).

OS.q: Why is the Optimal page replacement algorithm not used in practice?
opts: It requires future knowledge of the reference string
It has the highest fault rate
OS.exp: Optimal replaces the page not used for the longest time in the FUTURE, which an OS cannot know; it serves as a benchmark.

OS.q: LRU replaces the page that:
opts: Will not be used for the longest time in the future
OS.exp: LRU replaces the least recently used page, based on past access history.

OS.q: Virtual memory allows:
opts: Processes to execute even when they cannot fit entirely in physical memory
OS.exp: Virtual memory enables processes to execute outside of memory — larger than physical RAM allows.

OS.q: Demand paging specifies that:
opts: All pages are always in memory
If a memory region is not being used, it is swapped to disk to make room for other applications
OS.exp: Demand paging swaps out unused memory regions to disk so applications can use RAM they need now.

OS.q: Disk Access Time equals:
opts: Seek time + rotational latency + transfer time
OS.exp: Access time = seek + rotational latency + transfer time.

OS.q: Seek time is:
opts: Time for the sector to rotate under the head
Time to position the disk arm on the desired track
OS.exp: Seek time is the time to locate the disk arm on the specified track.

OS.q: Rotational latency is:
opts: Time for the desired sector to rotate into position under the head
OS.exp: Rotational latency is the time taken for the desired sector to rotate into a readable position.

OS.q: Which disk scheduling algorithm behaves like an elevator?
OS.exp: SCAN moves the arm in one direction servicing requests, reverses at the end, and services on the return — the elevator algorithm.

OS.q: SSTF schedules requests based on:
opts: Shortest seek time from the current head position
OS.exp: SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) picks the request nearest to the current head position, minimising seek time.

OS.q: How does LOOK improve upon SCAN?
opts: Reverses at the last pending request instead of travelling to the disk's physical end
Always jumps to the far end
OS.exp: LOOK avoids the wasted traversal to the disk edge by reversing direction at the last request in front of the head.

OS.q: CLOOK differs from LOOK in that:
opts: It moves in one direction and then jumps to the other end's last request rather than reversing
It ignores requests behind the head
OS.exp: CLOOK, like CSCAN, is one-directional; after serving the last request on the way, it jumps to the last request at the other end.

OS.q: A kernel that contains all OS code in a single executable image is called:
OS.exp: A monolithic kernel packs all OS services into one image; microkernel runs only minimal services; macro kernel combines both.

OS.q: A microkernel runs:
opts: All OS services in kernel space
Only minimal performance-affecting services in kernel space, with the rest handled by processes
OS.exp: Microkernels keep the kernel small — running only minimal services — and delegate the rest to user-mode processes.

OS.q: Thrashing occurs when:
opts: The CPU executes too many user instructions
The processor spends most of its time swapping pages instead of executing instructions
Too many interrupts arrive per second
OS.exp: Thrashing is when excessive paging in a virtual-memory system collapses useful throughput.

OS.q: Which technique lets multiple users share a single copy of a program if the code cannot modify itself and each user's data is stored separately?
OS.exp: Re-entrancy is a memory-saving technique for multiprogrammed time-sharing systems.

OS.q: Aging is a technique used to:
OS.exp: Aging gradually raises the priority of long-waiting processes so they eventually get scheduled — solving starvation.

OS.q: Starvation in resource scheduling is:
opts: A waiting process not getting the resources it needs for a long time
OS.exp: Starvation: a process waits indefinitely because resources keep being allocated to others.

OS.q: Spooling is most closely associated with:
opts: Printing — queueing multiple applications' output jobs on disk
OS.exp: Spooling temporarily gathers data (classically print jobs) on disk and queues them to the device.

OS.q: Logical vs physical address space:
opts: Both are generated by the memory unit
Logical address is generated by the CPU; physical address is seen by the memory unit
Logical address is seen by hardware only
Physical address is generated at compile time
OS.exp: Logical addresses are CPU-generated (virtual); physical addresses are what the memory unit uses.

DBMS.q: A database is best defined as:
opts: A collection of related data representing some aspect of the real world
DBMS.exp: A database is a collection of related data representing some aspect of the real world, built and populated for a certain task.

DBMS.q: Which of the following is NOT a problem of file-processing systems that DBMS was designed to solve?
opts: Physical storage of data on disk
DBMS.exp: DBMS addresses redundancy, access difficulty, isolation, integrity, atomicity, concurrency and security. Physical storage exists in any file system.

DBMS.q: In an ER diagram, a weak entity set:
opts: Has a primary key underlined with a solid line
Lacks sufficient attributes for unique identification and uses a discriminator (dashed underline)
Must have a composite primary key
DBMS.exp: A weak entity set lacks a primary key; it has a partial key (discriminator) shown with a dashed underline and depends on a strong entity.

DBMS.q: A strong entity set is one that:
opts: Contains sufficient attributes to uniquely identify all its entities (has a primary key)
DBMS.exp: Strong entity sets have a primary key of their own, drawn as a solid underline.

DBMS.q: A relationship set where three entity sets participate is called:
DBMS.exp: Ternary relationship sets involve exactly three participating entity sets.

DBMS.q: A relationship set where only one entity set participates is called:
DBMS.exp: Unary relationship sets have one participating entity set (also called recursive).

DBMS.q: 'One employee manages many departments, each managed by one employee' is which cardinality (employee → department)?
DBMS.exp: An A-entity relates to many B-entities, while each B-entity relates to at most one A-entity — one-to-many.

DBMS.q: 'Age' derived from 'Date of Birth' is an example of which attribute type?
DBMS.exp: Derived attributes are computed from other attributes.

DBMS.q: 'Name' composed of first, middle and last name is which attribute type?
DBMS.exp: Composite attributes are made up of several simple sub-attributes.

DBMS.q: A phone-number attribute holding multiple numbers per person is:
DBMS.exp: Multi-valued attributes can hold more than one value for a given entity.

DBMS.q: Which constraint states that no attribute of a primary key may be NULL?
DBMS.exp: Entity integrity requires primary-key attributes to be non-null.

DBMS.q: A foreign key value must:
opts: Either exist in the referenced relation's primary key or be NULL
DBMS.exp: Referential integrity: every foreign key is either present among the referenced primary key values or is NULL.

DBMS.q: A domain constraint specifies:
opts: The set of allowed values (atomic values from a domain) for an attribute
DBMS.exp: Domain constraints restrict the values (from an atomic domain) an attribute may take.

DBMS.q: Tuple uniqueness constraint specifies that:
opts: All primary key values are distinct
All tuples must be necessarily unique in any relation
DBMS.exp: Tuple uniqueness requires every tuple in a relation to be unique.

DBMS.q: A super key is:
opts: Any set of attributes that identifies each tuple uniquely (may include extra attributes)
DBMS.exp: Super key: any attribute set uniquely identifying tuples; a candidate key is a minimal super key.

DBMS.q: Which key is defined as a MINIMAL set of attributes that uniquely identifies each tuple?
DBMS.exp: A candidate key is a minimal super key.

DBMS.q: Candidate keys not chosen as the primary key are called:
DBMS.exp: Alternate keys are the unimplemented candidate keys.

DBMS.q: A primary key made of multiple attributes is called:
DBMS.exp: Composite key: primary key composed of multiple attributes.

DBMS.q: Which is true about a UNIQUE key (as distinct from a primary key)?
opts: May have a NULL value and is non-updatable once assigned
DBMS.exp: Unique keys allow NULL and, per the notes, are non-updatable once assigned.

DBMS.q: A functional dependency X → Y is trivial if and only if:
DBMS.exp: Trivial FD: RHS is a subset of LHS.

DBMS.q: Non-trivial FD X → Y means:
opts: At least one attribute of Y is not in X
DBMS.exp: Non-trivial: at least one RHS attribute is not in the LHS.

DBMS.q: The set of all attributes functionally determined by an attribute set is called its:
DBMS.exp: The closure X+ is everything functionally derivable from X.

DBMS.q: A decomposition of R into R1…Rn is LOSSLESS when:
DBMS.exp: Lossless join: natural join of sub-relations reproduces the original.

DBMS.q: A lossy join decomposition satisfies:
DBMS.exp: Lossy join: the natural join yields extra spurious tuples (superset of R).

DBMS.q: Dependency preservation ensures that:
opts: No FDs of the original relation are lost after decomposition
DBMS.exp: Dependency preservation keeps every original FD satisfied by the decomposed sub-relations.

DBMS.q: A relation is in 1NF if:
opts: Each cell contains only an atomic (or NULL) value
Every determinant is a super key
DBMS.exp: 1NF: attribute values are atomic (single-valued) or NULL.

DBMS.q: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and has no:
DBMS.exp: 2NF removes partial dependencies — proper subsets of a candidate key determining non-prime attributes.

DBMS.q: A → B is a transitive dependency (violating 3NF) when:
opts: A is a super key and B is prime
A is not a super key and B is a non-prime attribute
DBMS.exp: 3NF is violated when a non-super-key determines a non-prime attribute.

DBMS.q: BCNF requires that for every non-trivial FD A → B:
DBMS.exp: BCNF: the determinant of every non-trivial FD must be a super key.

DBMS.q: Read(A) in a transaction:
opts: Reads A from the database into a main-memory buffer
DBMS.exp: Read(A) reads A's value from the database and stores it in the buffer in main memory.

DBMS.q: Write(A) in a transaction:
opts: Writes A's updated buffer value back to the database
DBMS.exp: Write(A) writes the updated value of A from buffer to database.

DBMS.q: Which ACID property guarantees a transaction happens completely or not at all?
DBMS.exp: Atomicity forbids partial transactions.

DBMS.q: Which ACID property guarantees that database integrity constraints are maintained?
DBMS.exp: Consistency ensures the DB remains consistent before and after every transaction.

DBMS.q: Which ACID property ensures concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial ordering?
DBMS.exp: Isolation ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere; the outcome equals some serial execution.

DBMS.q: Durability ensures that:
opts: Committed changes are permanent and survive failures
DBMS.exp: Durability persists committed changes to disk permanently, surviving any failure.

DBMS.q: A transaction enters PARTIALLY COMMITTED state when:
opts: Its last instruction has executed but changes are still in the main-memory buffer
Its changes are written to disk
DBMS.exp: After the last instruction, changes are still buffered — partially committed.

DBMS.q: A transaction enters ABORTED state after:
DBMS.exp: After failure the changes are undone via rollback, then the transaction is aborted.

DBMS.q: The last state in a transaction's life cycle is:
DBMS.exp: After committed or aborted, transactions enter the terminated state — end of life cycle.

DBMS.q: Which schedules are ALWAYS consistent, recoverable, cascadeless and strict?
DBMS.exp: Serial schedules always have all four properties; non-serial ones may not.

DBMS.q: A non-serial schedule convertible to a serial one by swapping non-conflicting operations is:
DBMS.exp: That is the definition of conflict serializability.

DBMS.q: A schedule where T2 dirty-reads from uncommitted T1 and commits BEFORE T1 is:
DBMS.exp: If the reader commits before the writer it depended on, no rollback can save the read — irrecoverable.

DBMS.q: A cascading schedule is one where:
opts: Only one transaction runs at a time
Failure of one transaction causes several dependent transactions to roll back
Transactions run in reverse arrival order
DBMS.exp: Cascading rollback: aborting one transaction cascades to others that read its dirty data.

DBMS.q: In a strict schedule, a transaction:
opts: Is neither allowed to read nor write a data item until the last writer commits/aborts
DBMS.exp: Strict schedules delay both reads and writes until the previous writer commits or aborts.

DBMS.q: σ (Selection) operator:
DBMS.exp: Selection filters rows based on a predicate; projection filters columns.

DBMS.q: ∏ (Projection) operator:
DBMS.exp: Projection retains selected columns of a relation.

DBMS.q: Cross product of R1 (m rows) × R2 (n rows) returns how many rows?
DBMS.exp: Cross product yields every combination — m×n tuples.

DBMS.q: In relational algebra, minimum rows returned by R1 ∪ R2 (m,n rows) is:
DBMS.exp: Union returns at least max(m, n) tuples (if one set's tuples subset the other's) and at most m + n.

DBMS.q: R1 − R2 returns at most how many rows?
DBMS.exp: Difference R1 − R2 returns at most m rows (all of R1 if none are in R2).

DBMS.q: Natural join of two relations with NO common attribute equals:
DBMS.exp: Without a common attribute, no equality condition exists, so natural join becomes the Cartesian product.

DBMS.q: Which operator returns tuples of A associated with EVERY tuple of B?
DBMS.exp: Division answers 'for all' queries; B's attributes must be a proper subset of A's.

DBMS.q: Left outer join of R and S returns:
opts: All tuples of R and matching tuples of S (with NULLs for unmatched S)
All tuples of R and S with duplicates
DBMS.exp: LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps every tuple of R; unmatched S columns are NULL.

DBMS.q: Full outer join of R and S returns:
opts: Union of all tuples of R and S with NULLs in unmatched attributes
DBMS.exp: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps every tuple of both R and S with NULLs where unmatched.

DBMS.q: A clustering index is created on:
opts: A key field in an unordered file
A non-key field on which records are physically ordered
DBMS.exp: Clustering index is built on a non-key field on which the data file is physically ordered.

DBMS.q: A primary index is:
opts: An ordered file with (key, block-pointer) fields, matching primary-key ordering of data
An index on any non-key field
DBMS.exp: Primary index: ordered file with the primary key and a pointer to the data block containing that key.

DBMS.q: A secondary index:
opts: Provides additional access paths for a file for which primary access already exists
Is used only for range queries
DBMS.exp: Secondary indexes give additional means of accessing a file that already has primary access.

DBMS.q: Why is searching generally faster in a B+ tree than in a B tree?
opts: Non-leaf B+ nodes hold no record pointers, so they pack more keys and the tree is shallower
B+ trees store data only in the root
B trees do not allow range queries
DBMS.exp: B+ trees' internal nodes have higher fan-out, decreasing tree depth.

DBMS.q: The 'order' of a B-tree is:
opts: The maximum number of children a node can have
The number of keys in the root
DBMS.exp: Order = maximum number of children a node can have.

DBMS.q: In a B-tree of order P, the root can have between how many children?
DBMS.exp: Per the notes, the root can have between 2 and P children.

SQL.q: Which set of commands belongs to DDL?
SQL.exp: DDL defines schema structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME.

SQL.q: Which commands belong to DML?
SQL.exp: DML manipulates data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE.

SQL.q: GRANT and REVOKE belong to which language category?
SQL.exp: DCL controls permissions.

SQL.q: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT belong to which language category?
SQL.exp: TCL controls transactions.

SQL.q: Which command performs an UPSERT (insert or update) operation?
SQL.exp: MERGE is the DML statement for UPSERT semantics.

SQL.q: Which is the key difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
opts: DELETE removes the table structure; TRUNCATE does not
TRUNCATE removes all records and reclaims allocated space and is DDL; DELETE is DML and can use WHERE
SQL.exp: TRUNCATE (DDL) removes all rows including allocated space, no WHERE; DELETE (DML) removes selected rows, structure and space intact.

SQL.q: RENAME belongs to which category of SQL commands?
SQL.exp: RENAME (renaming an object) is a DDL command per the notes.

SQL.q: Which query returns only unique country values from Customers?
opts: SELECT Country FROM Customers GROUP BY *;
SQL.exp: SELECT DISTINCT returns only different values of the listed columns.

SQL.q: 'SELECT * FROM Customers;' means:
opts: Select all columns of all rows in Customers
SQL.exp: * is a wildcard for all columns.

SQL.q: How do you correctly test for NULL values?
SQL.exp: NULL cannot be compared with =/<>; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

SQL.q: Which is the correct 'not equal' operator in standard SQL?
SQL.exp: Standard SQL uses <> for not-equal; some dialects also accept !=.

SQL.q: An UPDATE statement without a WHERE clause will:
opts: Update every row in the table
SQL.exp: Omitting WHERE applies the SET clause to all rows — a classic interview trap.

SQL.q: A DELETE statement without a WHERE clause:
opts: Deletes all rows but leaves the table structure
SQL.exp: DELETE without WHERE removes all rows but preserves the table structure, attributes and indexes.

SQL.q: Which clause combines conditions such that a row must satisfy ALL of them?
SQL.exp: AND requires all connected conditions to be TRUE.

SQL.q: The NOT operator in a WHERE clause:
opts: Returns rows where the condition is FALSE
SQL.exp: NOT returns rows where the given condition is NOT TRUE.

SQL.q: 'ORDER BY Country ASC, CustomerName DESC' does:
opts: Sorts by Country ascending, ties broken by CustomerName descending
SQL.exp: Multiple ORDER BY columns sort hierarchically left to right.

SQL.q: By default, ORDER BY sorts:
SQL.exp: Default order is ascending; use DESC for descending.

SQL.q: Which pattern finds customer names with 'r' in the SECOND position?
SQL.exp: Underscore matches exactly one char; '_r%' = any first character, 'r' second, anything after.

SQL.q: What does 'LIKE a__%' match?
opts: Names starting with 'a', at least 2 characters
Names starting with 'a', at least 3 characters
SQL.exp: 'a' + two underscores + % → at least 3 characters starting with 'a'.

SQL.q: Which wildcard represents zero, one, or multiple characters in LIKE?
SQL.exp: % is zero-or-more characters; underscore is exactly one character.

SQL.q: WHERE Price BETWEEN 10 AND 20 selects:
SQL.exp: BETWEEN is inclusive of both endpoints.

SQL.q: WHERE Country IN ('Germany','France','UK') is shorthand for:
SQL.exp: IN acts as an OR-chained equality; can also take a subquery.

SQL.q: Which is a valid syntactic use of IN with a subquery?
opts: WHERE Country IN (SELECT Country FROM Suppliers)
WHERE Country IN SELECT Country FROM Suppliers
SQL.exp: IN accepts a value list or a SELECT statement enclosed in parentheses.

SQL.q: Inserting without listing column names requires:
opts: Values in the same order as the table's columns, one for each
SQL.exp: Omitting column list requires supplying values for every column in table column order.

SQL.q: Which is the syntax to update multiple columns?
opts: UPDATE t SET c1=v1 AND c2=v2 WHERE …
UPDATE t SET c1=v1, c2=v2 WHERE …
SQL.exp: Multiple SET assignments are separated by commas.

SQL.q: Which aggregate returns the number of rows matching a criterion?
SQL.exp: COUNT() counts rows.

SQL.q: MIN() returns:
opts: Smallest value of the selected column
SQL.exp: MIN() returns the smallest value of a column.

SQL.q: MAX() returns:
opts: Largest value of the selected column
SQL.exp: MAX() returns the largest value of a column.

SQL.q: AVG() returns:
SQL.exp: AVG() returns the average value of a numeric column.

SQL.q: SUM() returns:
opts: Total sum of a numeric column
SQL.exp: SUM() returns the total sum of a numeric column.

SQL.q: GROUP BY is used to:
opts: Group rows sharing values in one or more columns, typically with aggregates
SQL.exp: GROUP BY groups rows for aggregate summaries — often used with COUNT/SUM/MIN/MAX/AVG.

SQL.q: Why does SQL provide HAVING in addition to WHERE?
opts: WHERE cannot use aggregates; HAVING filters after grouping
SQL.exp: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters after GROUP BY using aggregates.

SQL.q: Which query lists countries having more than 5 customers?
opts: SELECT Country FROM Customers WHERE COUNT(CustomerID) > 5;
SELECT COUNT(CustomerID), Country FROM Customers GROUP BY Country HAVING COUNT(CustomerID) > 5;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Customers HAVING Country > 5;
SELECT Country FROM Customers GROUP BY COUNT(CustomerID) > 5;
SQL.exp: Aggregate filtering needs GROUP BY + HAVING; COUNT in WHERE is invalid.

SQL.q: Evaluation priority: which is given priority when both appear in a query?
SQL.exp: WHERE filters individual rows first; then GROUP BY groups; then HAVING filters groups.

SQL.q: Which JOIN returns only rows with matching values in BOTH tables?
SQL.exp: INNER JOIN keeps only matched rows.

SQL.q: In a LEFT JOIN of Customers (left) and Orders (right), a customer with no orders appears:
opts: With NULLs in the Orders columns
Once per existing order of others
SQL.exp: LEFT JOIN retains all left-table rows; unmatched right columns are NULL.

SQL.q: A RIGHT JOIN returns:
opts: All rows from the left table
All rows from the right table and matching rows from the left
SQL.exp: RIGHT JOIN keeps every right-table row, with NULLs for unmatched left columns.

SQL.q: A FULL OUTER JOIN returns:
opts: All rows from either table, with NULLs where no match exists
SQL.exp: FULL OUTER JOIN combines LEFT and RIGHT — keeps all rows of both tables with NULLs.

SQL.q: Which conditions must SELECTs meet to be combined with UNION?
opts: Same number of columns, similar data types, same column order
SQL.exp: UNION requires equal column count, compatible data types, same order.

SQL.q: Difference between UNION and UNION ALL:
opts: UNION selects only distinct values by default; UNION ALL allows duplicates
UNION is faster than UNION ALL
SQL.exp: UNION deduplicates the combined result; UNION ALL preserves duplicates, so it is typically faster.

SQL.q: Which are equivalent ways (across DB systems) to fetch the first 3 rows?
opts: SELECT TOP 3 …, LIMIT 3, FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY, ROWNUM <= 3
SQL.exp: SQL Server uses TOP, MySQL uses LIMIT, standard SQL/DB2/Oracle 12c+ use FETCH FIRST, older Oracle uses ROWNUM.

SQL.q: 'ALTER TABLE Customers ADD Email varchar(255);' does what?
opts: Adds a new column Email to the existing Customers table
SQL.exp: ALTER TABLE ADD adds a column; DROP COLUMN removes; MODIFY/ALTER COLUMN changes datatype.

SQL.q: 'ALTER TABLE Customers DROP COLUMN Email;' does what?
opts: Deletes the Email column from the table
Removes rows where Email is NULL
SQL.exp: DROP COLUMN removes an entire column and its data.

SQL.q: 'ALTER TABLE Persons ALTER COLUMN DateOfBirth year;' does what?
SQL.exp: ALTER/MODIFY COLUMN changes a column's data type.

SQL.q: CREATE DATABASE is used to:
SQL.exp: CREATE DATABASE creates a new database (DDL).

SQL.q: DROP DATABASE:
SQL.exp: DROP DATABASE removes an existing database entirely.

SQL.q: DROP TABLE:
opts: Removes all rows but keeps the table
SQL.exp: DROP TABLE removes the table entirely.

SQL.q: TRUNCATE TABLE:
opts: Deletes all rows but preserves the table structure
SQL.exp: TRUNCATE removes all rows and reclaims space; table structure remains.

SQL.q: Which TCL command permanently saves the current transaction's changes?
SQL.exp: COMMIT commits a transaction, persisting its changes.

SQL.q: Which TCL command undoes a transaction on error?
SQL.exp: ROLLBACK reverts the transaction's changes on error.

SQL.q: Which TCL command creates an intermediate point to roll back to?
SQL.exp: SAVEPOINT marks a point in a transaction; ROLLBACK TO savepoint undoes work after it.

SQL.q: GRANT and REVOKE are used to:
opts: Give and withdraw access privileges to database users
SQL.exp: GRANT provides privileges; REVOKE withdraws them (both DCL).
